Chapter 5 · 第五章

Unlocking the Power of Feedback释放反馈的力量

— PDF p.123 —

A Note on Terminology术语说明

In this chapter, I'll refer to two types of feedback—positive and constructive:

本章中，我会提到两类反馈——正面反馈与建设性反馈：

Positive (or reinforcing) feedback: This feedback highlights what someone is doing well, reinforces good habits, and builds confidence.

正面（或强化性）反馈：这类反馈指出某人做得好的地方，巩固良好的习惯，并建立信心。

Constructive feedback: This feedback focuses on surfacing blind spots, helping someone overcome challenges, or encouraging new behaviors.

建设性反馈：这类反馈侧重于指出盲区、帮助某人克服挑战，或鼓励新的行为。

Technically, both are constructive: they contribute to someone's growth. But in this chapter, when I say constructive feedback, I'll mostly be referring to improvement-focused feedback: the kind that helps someone see what to do differently or better.

从技术上讲，两者都是建设性的：它们都有助于一个人的成长。但在本章中，当我说到"建设性反馈"时，大多指的是"以改进为导向"的反馈：那种帮助对方看清该如何做得不同、做得更好的反馈。

As a tech lead, one of your primary responsibilities is helping your team members grow. There's a whole toolkit available to you with items like mentoring, sharing knowledge, and delegation, but none are as impactful as feedback. Yet, despite its power, feedback is often underutilized or mishandled.

作为技术负责人，你的首要职责之一就是帮助团队成员成长。你手边有一整套工具，比如导师辅导、知识分享和授权委派，但没有哪一样比反馈更有影响力。然而，尽管反馈如此强大，它却常常被忽视或处理失当。

I see it all the time: tech leads who shy away from giving feedback because they're afraid of damaging relationships or pushing cultural boundaries, or they're unsure how to approach it. They worry that giving constructive feedback will make them seem harsh or unkind or jeopardize trust they've worked hard to build. So they stay quiet, hoping the issue will resolve itself; often, though, it just tends to fester.

这种情形我屡见不鲜：技术负责人回避给出反馈，因为他们怕破坏关系、怕触碰文化边界，或者不知道该怎么开口。他们担心给出建设性反馈会让自己显得刻薄或不近人情，或是危及好不容易建立起来的信任。于是他们选择沉默，指望问题自己消失；可往往事与愿违，问题只会不断恶化。

— PDF p.124 —

On the other hand, there are those who deliver feedback carelessly, leaving team members discouraged or questioning their abilities. The issue isn't that feedback doesn't work; it's that feedback, when done poorly, can backfire. It can harm relationships, damage careers, and demotivate someone entirely. But when done right, feedback can be transformative.

另一方面，也有人随随便便地给出反馈，让团队成员灰心丧气，甚至怀疑自己的能力。问题不在于反馈没用，而在于反馈一旦做得糟糕，就会适得其反。它可能伤害关系、断送职业前景、彻底打垮一个人的积极性。但只要做得得当，反馈也能带来脱胎换骨的改变。

Even the smallest comments can have a profound impact. A simple "Great presentation today!" can boost someone's confidence, reassuring them they're on the right track. Constructive feedback, delivered thoughtfully and with clear examples, can save someone years of heading in the wrong direction. It can help someone see what they might be missing and encourage real progress. I've seen it happen time and time again, and I've experienced it myself.

哪怕是最微小的一句话，也可能产生深远的影响。一句简单的"今天的汇报很棒！"就能提振某人的信心，让他确信自己走在正确的路上。而经过深思熟虑、辅以清晰例子的建设性反馈，则可能帮一个人省下好几年在错误方向上摸索的时间。它能让人看清自己可能忽略的东西，并推动真正的进步。这样的事我见过一次又一次，我自己也亲身经历过。

I'll never forget a moment that changed the way I thought about leadership. My tech lead sat me down for a thoughtful conversation about how I was showing up at work, especially in my interactions with other team members. He walked me through a few examples, pointed out some patterns, and gently helped me see the impact I was having.

我永远忘不了那个改变了我对领导力看法的时刻。我的技术负责人把我叫到一旁，就我在工作中的表现——尤其是我和其他团队成员的互动方式——进行了一次深入的谈话。他给我举了几个例子，指出了一些行为模式，温和地帮我看清自己造成的影响。

The main message he shared, though not in these exact words, was clear: I was lacking emotional intelligence, and if I wanted to lead tech teams effectively, I needed to start developing it.

他传达的核心意思——虽然不是用的原话——很清楚：我缺乏情商，而如果我想有效地带好技术团队，就必须开始培养它。

Even though he delivered it with care and context, it still hurt. But it was also a turning point. It made me look inward and start focusing on how my behavior impacted others, rather than just fixating on metrics, results, and code. That piece of feedback was a game-changer, not just for my development as a leader but for my entire career, to the point that now I'm a huge advocate for soft skills in tech, and I am helping others develop theirs.

尽管他表达时很体贴、也铺垫了背景，这话还是让我难受。但它同时也是一个转折点。它让我开始内省，开始关注自己的行为如何影响他人，而不再只是死盯着指标、结果和代码。那条反馈改变了游戏规则——不仅改变了我作为领导者的成长轨迹，也改变了我的整个职业生涯。以至于如今我成了技术领域"软技能"的坚定倡导者，并在帮助别人培养软技能。

Or the time I told a senior developer on my team that his habit of constantly interrupting others was hurting their confidence and making them less likely to contribute. He had no idea the impact his behavior was having, but once I pointed it out, he was grateful and started addressing it. Over time, his relationships with colleagues improved, people's perception of him shifted, and even the quality of his work benefited. As his relationships deepened and trust grew, the other team members felt more comfortable engaging with him, giving him honest feedback, and collaborating more openly. This not only improved his awareness of how others perceived him but also gave him more opportunities to learn and refine his approach, ultimately elevating the quality of his contributions.

又比如有一次，我告诉团队里一位资深开发：他总爱打断别人的习惯，正在打击对方的信心，让对方越来越不敢发言。他完全没意识到自己的行为造成了这样的影响，但经我指出后，他心怀感激并着手改进。久而久之，他和同事的关系改善了，大家对他的看法也转变了，甚至连他工作的质量都跟着受益。随着关系加深、信任增长，其他团队成员更愿意和他交流、更敢于给他诚实的反馈、也更开放地与他协作。这不仅提升了他对"别人如何看待自己"的认知，也给了他更多学习和改进方式的机会，最终让他的产出质量更上一层楼。

— PDF p.125 —

Feedback isn't just about what you deliver yourself; it's also about encouraging others to use it. Imagine two team members in a continuous conflict, and one of them comes to you frustrated and saying "Every time I speak in meetings, he cuts me off." My first response would be to encourage them to give feedback directly to the other person, explaining how having the courage to address things openly can not only help resolve the current conflict but also strengthen their relationship and reduce future misunderstandings. I would also offer to coach them through preparing the feedback and delivering it in a way that feels authentic and comfortable for them. Often, the other person isn't even aware of the impact they're having, and hearing it can lead to a meaningful change.

反馈不只是你自己去给出，还包括鼓励别人也去使用反馈。设想两位团队成员长期冲突，其中一方带着委屈来找你说："每次我在会上发言，他都打断我。"我的第一反应会是鼓励他直接向对方反馈，并向他解释：鼓起勇气把事情摊开来讲，不仅有助于化解眼下的冲突，还能巩固彼此的关系、减少未来的误解。我也会主动辅导他如何准备这段反馈，并以一种让他觉得真诚、自在的方式表达出来。很多时候，对方根本没意识到自己造成的影响，而一旦听到，就可能带来有意义的改变。

By teaching your team the power of feedback and encouraging them to use it regularly, you amplify its effects and create a feedback culture. In this kind of culture, people push themselves, and each other, to grow. Positive feedback acknowledges contributions and boosts morale, while improvement-focused feedback highlights gaps and offers a path forward. Making use of both types of feedback consistently helps build stronger relationships, improve team performance, and keep the team motivated. And best of all, this magic happens even when you're not around.

通过教会团队反馈的力量、并鼓励他们经常使用，你就能放大反馈的效果，营造出一种反馈文化。在这种文化里，人们会推动自己、也推动彼此去成长。正面反馈认可贡献、提振士气，而以改进为导向的反馈指出差距、指明前路。持续地善用这两类反馈，有助于建立更牢固的关系、提升团队绩效、保持团队的动力。最妙的是，即便你不在场，这种魔力依然在发挥作用。

Giving feedback isn't always easy, especially when it's improvement-focused and touches on areas the other person needs to work on. It takes thought, care, and practice. Even with careful preparation, it can feel risky because you never know how the other person will respond. No wonder so many tech leads avoid it, putting it off until it's absolutely necessary! But delaying improvement feedback just because it's uncomfortable means missing an opportunity to help someone grow. It also increases the risk of the situation escalating if the behavior isn't addressed early. I cover this in more detail in the section "Understanding the Five Principles of Good Feedback" on page 117.

给出反馈并不总是容易的事，尤其是当它以改进为导向、触及对方需要下功夫的方面时。这需要思考、用心和练习。即便准备充分，它仍可能让人觉得有风险，因为你永远不知道对方会作何反应。难怪那么多技术负责人回避它，一拖再拖、直到万不得已！但仅仅因为不舒服就推迟改进反馈，意味着错失了一次帮助别人成长的机会。如果不趁早处理，行为不被纠正，还会让局面升级的风险加大。我在第 117 页"理解良好反馈的五项原则"一节中有更详细的论述。

This chapter is here to make giving and receiving feedback less intimidating and give you practical ways to use it effectively.

本章的目的，就是让"给出反馈"和"接收反馈"都不再那么令人畏惧，并给你一些切实可用的方法，把反馈真正用起来。

How to Get Useful Feedback from Your Team如何从团队那里获得有用的反馈

Getting useful feedback from your team isn't easy. It takes effort because it involves people being open, risking vulnerability, and possibly stepping into conflict. These are uncomfortable dynamics for most people, and in tech environments, where the focus often leans heavily on logic and execution, they can feel especially unfamiliar. Add the authority piece that comes with being a tech lead, and it's 10 times harder.

从团队那里获得有用的反馈并不容易。这需要付出努力，因为它要求人们敞开心扉、冒着暴露脆弱的风险，甚至可能直面冲突。对大多数人来说，这些都是令人不自在的互动方式；而在技术环境里——当重心往往过度偏向逻辑和执行时——它们更显得格格不入。再叠加技术负责人身上自带的权威光环，难度直接翻了十倍。

— PDF p.126 —

When it comes to positive feedback, people often assume you don't need it. "Of course you're doing a good job," they think. "That's why you're leading the team." They don't realize how valuable a simple acknowledgment can be for your motivation.

说到正面反馈，人们常常想当然地认为你并不需要它。"你当然做得不错，"他们心里想，"不然怎么会是你在带团队呢。"他们没意识到，一句简单的认可对你的动力有多么宝贵。

Improvement feedback is even trickier. People are often hesitant to share it with their tech lead because they're not sure how you'll react, or they worry there could be negative consequences for them. Or sometimes, they just don't know how to give feedback in a helpful way.

改进类的反馈就更棘手了。人们往往不愿把它告诉自己的技术负责人，因为他们拿不准你会作何反应，或者担心会给自己带来负面后果。又或者，他们只是不知道该怎么以一种有帮助的方式给出反馈。

If you want feedback that helps you grow, whether it's encouragement or constructive critique, you need to make it happen. Build trust with your team, show them how valuable their input is, and guide them on how to give feedback that's actionable.

如果你想要有助于自己成长的反馈——无论是鼓励还是建设性的批评——你就得主动去促成它。与团队建立信任，让他们看到自己的意见有多宝贵，并引导他们如何给出可落地的反馈。

In this section, I'll share simple, practical strategies you can apply immediately to get the kind of feedback that makes a difference.

在本节中，我会分享一些简单、实用的策略，你可以立刻上手，去获得那种真正能带来改变的反馈。

HOW TO ASK FOR FEEDBACK如何请求反馈

The way you ask for feedback has a huge impact on what you get back. If you want feedback that's helpful and actionable, you need to put effort into the process and prepare for it. The key is to be clear, specific, and intentional about what you're asking for.

你请求反馈的方式，会极大地影响你最终得到什么。如果你想要的是有帮助、可落地的反馈，就得在这个过程中投入精力、提前准备。关键在于：对你所问的内容，要清晰、具体、有意图。

Start by being straightforward about the areas where you need input. Asking vague questions like "Do you have any feedback for me?" often leads to vague answers. Instead, focus on something concrete: "I've been working on improving my feedback skills. What do you think I could do to improve further?" or "I'm struggling with delegating effectively. How do you think I'm doing?" When you're honest about what you're working on, it signals to your team that you're open to feedback, and removes the awkward guesswork about what they think you need to improve.

一开始就直接说出你需要别人在哪方面给你意见。像"你对我有什么反馈吗？"这种模糊的提问，往往只能换来模糊的回答。不如聚焦到具体的事情上："我一直在提升自己给反馈的能力，你觉得我还能在哪些方面做得更好？"或者"我一直不太擅长有效地授权，你觉得我做得怎么样？"当你坦诚地说出自己正在改进什么时，就向团队传递了你乐于接受反馈的信号，也省去了他们尴尬地猜测"你到底想让我们提哪方面"的麻烦。

If you're unsure about what specific area to focus on, you can ask for help identifying blind spots: "What's one thing I should start doing as a tech lead?" or "What's one thing I could do to better support the team?" These open-ended but targeted questions give people room to offer insights without feeling pressured.

如果你不确定该聚焦哪个具体方面，可以请对方帮你找出盲区："作为技术负责人，有哪件事是我应该开始做的？"或者"我可以做哪一件事来更好地支持团队？"这些开放式但有针对性的问题，给了对方畅所欲言的空间，又不会让他们感到压力。

To make feedback even more specific, use the 1-to-10 scaling system. For example, ask, "On a scale of 1 to 10, how good do you think I am at giving feedback?" If they rate you a 10, ask why: "What am I doing that makes you think I'm a 10?" If they give a lower number, ask what's missing: "What do you think I need to work on to reach a 10?" The number itself doesn't matter; it's all about the conversation it triggers. People find it easier to share their thoughts when they can anchor them to a scale, and it helps you pinpoint actionable steps for growth.

想让反馈更具体，可以用 1 到 10 分的评分法。例如问："如果用 1 到 10 打分，你觉得我给反馈的能力能打几分？"如果对方给你打 10 分，就追问为什么："我做了什么让你觉得我能到 10 分？"如果给了较低的分数，就问缺在哪："你觉得我要在哪些方面下功夫才能到 10 分？"分数本身并不重要，重要的是它所引发的对话。当人们能把想法锚定在一个量表上时，会更容易说出口；这也帮你精准定位出可以落地的成长步骤。

— PDF p.127 —

Who you ask for feedback is just as important as how you ask. Don't limit yourself to one group; seek input from everyone around you. You want to make sure you are getting input from both people who challenge you and those who cheer you on. Your team members can offer valuable insights about your day-to-day interactions, stakeholders can provide a broader perspective on how your leadership is perceived, and mentors can give you strategic advice.

你向谁请教反馈，和你怎么请教同样重要。不要把自己局限在某一群人里；要向身边所有人征求意见。你要确保既听到那些敢于挑战你的人的声音，也听到那些为你加油打气的人的声音。团队成员能就你日常的互动提供宝贵的洞察；干系人能就"你的领导方式在别人眼中如何"提供更宏观的视角；导师则能给你战略性的建议。

When to ask also matters. Don't surprise people with feedback requests. Give them time to think. For example, mention in your one-on-ones on a given week that you'd like to have a feedback session next week, and share the topics you'd like their input on. Sending an email in advance can also help: explain why their feedback matters to you, outline the areas you want to discuss, and remind them to prepare. Avoid pulling people into an impromptu meeting with a vague "I just wanted to get some feedback."

什么时候问也很关键。不要用反馈请求去突袭别人。给他们时间思考。例如，可以在某一周的一对一里提一句，说你想在下周安排一次反馈沟通，并把你希望他们给意见的话题分享出来。提前发封邮件也有帮助：说明他们的反馈对你为什么重要、列出你想讨论的方面，并提醒他们做些准备。避免把人临时拉进一个会，然后模糊地来一句"我就是想听听反馈"。

Another good moment to ask for feedback is during offboarding. When someone is leaving the team, whether for a new role, a different company, or even just an internal move, they're often more reflective and more willing to share open, honest observations. Use that window to ask what worked well, what frustrated them, and how you showed up as a leader. A thoughtful offboarding conversation can surface insights you may not hear otherwise and help you improve the environment for the rest of your team.

另一个征求反馈的好时机是离职面谈。当有人要离开团队时——无论是去新岗位、去别的公司，甚至只是内部转岗——他们往往更愿意反思、也更敢于开诚布公地分享观察。利用这个窗口去问：哪些方面做得好、哪些让他们感到受挫、以及你作为领导者表现得如何。一次用心的离职谈话，能让你听到平时听不到的洞察，帮你为留下的人改善环境。

Finally, treat feedback as a priority by scheduling it properly. Block time on their calendar, and include a note explaining the purpose of the meeting and the specific areas you'd like to discuss. This shows that you value their input and sets the tone for a productive conversation. A simple touch like this can make all the difference in getting the feedback you need to grow.

最后，把反馈当作一件重要的事来认真排期。在他们的日历上留出时间，并附上说明，写清会议目的以及你想讨论的具体方面。这表明你重视他们的意见，也为一次富有成效的对话定下基调。这样一个简单的举动，往往就能决定你能否获得成长所需的反馈。

Asking for feedback intentionally creates the conditions for honesty, thoughtfulness, and trust.

有意识地去请求反馈，就为坦诚、深思熟虑和信任创造了条件。

HOW TO RECEIVE FEEDBACK如何接收反馈

The feedback, both positive and constructive, starts flowing in. Now what? How you receive feedback matters just as much as how you give it. In fact, it sets the tone for how others approach feedback in your team. If you want people to be open to feedback and grateful for it, you need to model that behavior yourself.

正面的和建设性的反馈开始涌入了。接下来怎么办？你如何接收反馈，和你如何给出反馈同样重要。事实上，你接收反馈的方式，为团队里其他人如何对待反馈定下了基调。如果你希望大家乐于接受反馈、并心怀感激，那你自己就得以身作则。

Start with gratitude. Whatever feedback you're hearing, whether you like it or not, remember that someone has put effort into sharing it with you. A simple "Thank you for taking the time to share this with me" goes a long way. Acknowledging feedback doesn't mean you have to agree with it; it simply shows respect for the effort and the intention behind it.

从感恩开始。无论你听到的是什么反馈、无论你喜不喜欢，都要记住：有人花了心力来和你分享。一句简单的"谢谢你抽出时间和我说这些"，效果会远超你的想象。认可反馈并不意味着你必须赞同它；它只是表达你对这份付出和背后心意的尊重。

— PDF p.128 —

Next, validate the feedback. This means making sure you understand it fully. Ask clarifying questions like "Let me see if I got this right. Are you saying that…?" or "What do you mean by that?" If the feedback is vague or unclear, ask for specific examples: "Can you give me an example of when this happened?" Context is everything when it comes to feedback, and understanding the specifics will help you decide how to act on it.

接下来，要确认你真正理解了反馈。这意味着要确保你完全听懂了。可以问一些澄清性的问题，比如"我确认一下我理解得对不对。你的意思是说……？"或者"你这么说指的是什么？"如果反馈含糊不清，就请对方举具体例子："能给我举一个这件事发生时的例子吗？"在反馈这件事上，上下文就是一切；弄清具体细节，才能帮你决定该如何行动。

One time, I saw a tech lead dive headfirst into a complex conflict because she assumed what someone's feedback meant and jumped straight to action instead of taking the time to dig deeper. A team member had approached her with feedback: "I think you should code more as a tech lead." She took it to heart, immediately apologized, and started explaining herself. She then spent time reworking her schedule to increase her coding hours. But despite the adjustment and all the effort she put into it, the same feedback came up again from the same person in their next session.

有一次，我看到一位技术负责人一头扎进了一场复杂的矛盾里——因为她想当然地理解了别人反馈的意思，没有花时间深究，就直接采取了行动。一位团队成员曾给她这样的反馈："我觉得作为技术负责人，你应该多写点代码。"她把这话当了真，立刻道歉，开始为自己辩解，然后花时间重新调整日程、增加写代码的时间。可尽管做了调整、也付出了那么多努力，下一次沟通时，同一个人又提出了同样的反馈。

This time, instead of rushing to fix it, she dug deeper: "Why do you feel that way?" The response was revealing: "Because my previous tech lead used to code way more." She pressed further, asking, "How do you think me coding more would help you or the team?" The answer caught her off guard: "I don't know, but you asked for an area of improvement, and this is what I came up with." Finally, she asked, "How much more coding do you think I should be doing?" The team member replied, "At my last company, my tech lead knew every piece of the code and even coded overtime."

这一次，她没有急着去"补救"，而是往深里问："你为什么会这么觉得？"对方的回答很说明问题："因为我上一任技术负责人写代码多多了。"她继续追问："你觉得我多写代码，会怎么帮到你或团队？"答案让她始料未及："我不知道，可你让我提一个可以改进的方面，我就想到了这个。"最后她问："那你觉得我应该多写多少代码？"这位团队成员答道："在我上一家公司，我的技术负责人对每一行代码都了如指掌，甚至还加班写代码。"

That's when it hit her. The problem wasn't that she wasn't coding enough; it was a misalignment of expectations about her role as a tech lead. By rushing to action, she had been trying to solve the wrong problem. So, she changed her approach. She took the opportunity to explain what the tech lead role entailed at this company, how it differed from what he'd experienced before, and why coding wasn't her primary responsibility. She also shared the many other tasks on her plate that didn't allow her to code as much as the rest of the team. The team member thanked her for taking the time to clarify, and the feedback never came up again.

这时她才恍然大悟。问题不在于她代码写得不够多，而在于双方对"技术负责人这一角色"的预期不一致。由于急于行动，她一直在试图解决一个错误的问题。于是她改变了做法。她借此机会解释：在这家公司，技术负责人这个角色究竟意味着什么、和他以前经历的有何不同、以及为什么写代码并不是她的首要职责。她还分享了自己手头那一大堆让她无法像团队其他人那样多写代码的工作。这位团队成员感谢她花时间澄清，此后那条反馈再也没被提起过。

This story highlights the importance of validating feedback before reacting to it.

这个故事凸显了：在对反馈做出反应之前，先确认它，有多么重要。

— PDF p.129 —

Think about how you approach architectural decisions or feature requests. You'd never jump in and start building something based on a vague prompt; you'd probably ask questions, clarify goals, and make sure you understood the problem first. The same principle applies here: asking clarifying questions helps you understand the real concern and respond in a way that's thoughtful and aligned with the actual issue.

想想你平时是怎么处理架构决策或功能需求的。你绝不会凭着一句含糊的提示就一头扎进去开始动手；你多半会先提问、澄清目标，确保自己真正理解了问题。同样的原则在这里也适用：提出澄清性的问题，能帮你理解真正的关切所在，从而以一种深思熟虑、切中实际问题的方式去回应。

Let's explore some common scenarios and how to handle them:

我们来看看几种常见情形，以及该如何应对：

When positive feedback isn't new当正面反馈并不新鲜时

If someone tells you something you're already known for, something you're a natural at, or one of your commonly recognized strengths, like "You're great at facilitating meetings" or "You're great at breaking down complex problems for the team," don't just brush it off. Instead, dig deeper: "Why do you think it's important for me to keep doing this?" or "How does this action help you or the team?" Even familiar positive feedback can provide valuable insight into the impact of your strengths and reinforce behaviors worth continuing.

如果有人告诉你的，是你早已为人所知的长处、你天生擅长的事，或是大家公认的优点——比如"你特别擅长主持会议"或"你特别擅长为团队拆解复杂问题"——不要一笑置之。相反，往深里问："你觉得我继续做这件事为什么重要？"或者"这样做对你或团队有什么帮助？"即便是听来熟悉的正面反馈，也能让你宝贵地洞察到自己的优势所产生的影响，并强化那些值得继续保持的行为。

When you don't like what you hear当你不喜欢听到的内容时

It's natural to feel defensive when you receive feedback that stings or contradicts your self-perception. For example, someone might say, "You come across as dismissive in meetings." But you might not see yourself that way at all; you might feel like you're always encouraging input and exploring multiple perspectives. Comments like this can catch you off guard, and your instinct might be to explain yourself or push back.

当你收到刺耳的、或与自我认知相矛盾的反馈时，感到自我防御是很自然的。例如，有人可能说："你在会上给人一种不屑一顾的感觉。"可你也许完全不觉得自己是那样；你可能觉得自己一直在鼓励大家发言、在探索多种视角。这样的话会让你猝不及防，你的本能反应可能是为自己辩解或反驳。

But resist that urge. Instead, stay curious. Ask clarifying questions like, "Can you tell me more about this?" or "Could you give me an example of this behavior?" Even if you don't agree with the feedback, understanding the perspective behind it can be incredibly valuable. There may be a gap between how you see yourself and how others experience you, and that's exactly where valuable learning can happen.

但请克制住那种冲动。取而代之，保持好奇。问一些澄清性的问题，比如："能多和我讲讲这一点吗？"或者"能给我举一个这种行为的例子吗？"即便你不认同这条反馈，理解它背后的视角也可能极有价值。你眼中的自己，和别人实际体验到的你之间，可能存在落差；而恰恰在这种落差里，才能发生宝贵的学习。

Another common example that can trigger defensiveness is when someone gives you feedback about something you said or joked about that made them uncomfortable.

另一个容易触发自我防御的常见情形是：有人就你说过的某句话、或开过的某个玩笑给你反馈，说那让他们不舒服。

Let's say you made an inappropriate joke that didn't sit well with someone on your team. They let you know it made them feel uncomfortable. It's tempting to respond with "That's not what I meant!" or "It was just a joke." But doing that invalidates their experience and shuts down the conversation.

假设你开了一个不太合适的玩笑，让团队里某个人心里很不舒服。他们让你知道这让他们感到别扭。你很想回一句"我不是那个意思！"或者"不就是开个玩笑嘛。"但这样做等于否定了他们的感受，也让对话戛然而止。

— PDF p.130 —

Instead, acknowledge what they're telling you and own the impact. You might say, "I hear you. I'm really sorry it came across that way. It wasn't my intention, but I understand it made you uncomfortable. I'll be more mindful next time."

相反，你应当承认他们告诉你的感受，并为造成的影响负责。你可以这样说："我听到了。很抱歉让你产生了那样的感受。那不是我的本意，但我理解它让你不舒服了。下次我会更加注意。"

In moments like these, your intention doesn't matter as much as the impact. You don't need to defend yourself; just take the feedback seriously, thank them for raising it, and commit to doing better.

在这样的时刻，你的"本意"远不如"造成的影响"重要。你不必为自己辩护；只要认真对待这条反馈、感谢他们提出来、并承诺会做得更好就好。

When you're unsure how to react当你不确定该如何反应时

They just throw some raw, unstructured, or completely unexpected feedback at you, like "I think you handled that situation really badly." It might come out of nowhere, catch you off guard, or be hard to make sense of in the moment.

别人突然丢给你一句未经铺垫、毫无条理、或完全出乎意料的反馈，比如"我觉得你那件事处理得很糟"。它可能凭空冒出来、让你措手不及，或者当场根本无从理解。

You can't always control how or when feedback is delivered, but you can control how you respond. In this case, it's OK to say, "I need some time to think about this. I'll come back to you." This shows that you take the feedback seriously and gives you the space to process it without rushing into a reaction.

你无法总是控制反馈以何种方式、在何时被递到你面前，但你可以控制自己如何回应。这种情况下，你完全可以说："这件事我需要一点时间想想，我回头再找你。"这既表明你认真对待了反馈，也给你留出了消化它的空间，而不必仓促做出反应。

During the feedback session, avoid interrupting the person sharing their thoughts. If you have questions, jot them down and ask them once they're done.

在反馈沟通的过程中，不要打断正在分享想法的人。如果你有问题，先记下来，等他们说完再问。

Remember, receiving feedback doesn't mean you have to agree with everything. What matters most is staying open and curious and making an effort to understand the other person's perspective. You don't have to act on every piece of feedback, but by listening thoughtfully and engaging in a meaningful conversation, you'll build trust and encourage others to continue sharing their insights with you.

请记住，接收反馈并不意味着你必须全盘接受。最重要的是保持开放和好奇，努力去理解对方的视角。你不必对每一条反馈都照做，但通过用心倾听、进行有意义的对话，你会建立起信任，并鼓励别人继续和你分享他们的见解。

WHAT TO DO WITH THE RECEIVED FEEDBACK如何处理收到的反馈

To make the most of it, all feedback should be tracked and documented. This isn't just helpful for performance reviews; it's also a powerful way to track your progress over time. It allows you to see how others perceive your growth and areas of improvement.

为了让反馈发挥最大价值，所有反馈都应当被记录和留存。这不仅对绩效评估有用，也是一种随时间追踪自己进步的有力方式。它让你能看到别人如何看待你的成长、以及你需要改进的方面。

One of the simplest methods I recommend is creating an online document titled My Feedback. Use this to record every piece of feedback you receive, including the context, who gave it to you, and the date. Keep it easily accessible so you can revisit it regularly and reflect on your journey. Personally, I believe it's best if you take the notes yourself during feedback sessions, even in a remote environment (small comments that will help you remember what's important; you don't need the whole transcript). While some prefer using AI assistants to transcribe conversations, I find this can make the exchange feel less personal and even inhibit open dialogue. Plus, knowing you're being recorded might make some team members hesitate to speak freely. Always ask your team what they're comfortable with before introducing tools like this.

我推荐的最简单方法之一，是建一份名为 My Feedback 的在线文档。用它记录你收到的每一条反馈，包括当时的情境、是谁给的、以及日期。把它放在随手可及的地方，这样你就能定期回顾、反思自己的历程。就我个人而言，我认为最好是你自己在反馈沟通中亲手记录——即便在远程环境下也是如此（记几句关键的小要点，帮你记住重要的东西就行，不必逐字逐句）。虽然有些人喜欢用 AI 助手来转录对话，但我发现这会让交流显得不那么有人情味，甚至抑制坦诚的对话。而且，知道自己被录音，可能会让一些团队成员不敢畅所欲言。在引入这类工具之前，一定要先问问团队他们觉得怎样自在。

— PDF p.131 —

Once you've collected feedback, the next step is to analyze it. Start by inspecting the feedback to identify what's useful. Ask yourself, "What's new information?," "What feedback has been repeated?," "What can I directly apply?," and "How valuable is this to me and my goals?"

收集到反馈之后，下一步是分析它。先把反馈过一遍，找出哪些是有用的。问问自己："哪些是新信息？""哪些反馈被反复提到了？""哪些我可以直接用上？"以及"这条反馈对我和我的目标有多大价值？"

Then, refine it into something actionable. Feedback like "You need to improve your communication" is too broad to act on. Look for patterns or ask clarifying questions to get to the root behavior. Maybe it's "You tend to speak too quickly in meetings" or "You don't summarize decisions before moving on." The more specific you get, the easier it is to take meaningful action.

然后，把它打磨成可落地的东西。像"你需要改进沟通"这样的反馈，太宽泛，根本没法据此行动。要去找规律，或问一些澄清性问题，挖到行为的根上。也许真正的问题是"你在会上往往说得太快"，或者"你在进入下一项之前从不总结刚才的决定"。你越具体，就越容易采取有意义的行动。

From there, make a plan. For areas you want to improve, define what success looks like and outline next steps. That could mean adjusting a habit, practicing a skill, or setting up new feedback loops. Don't hesitate to ask for support if you're unsure how to implement the changes, from a peer, mentor, manager, or even an AI assistant. For example, you can prompt "Help me create a weekly plan to improve this feedback."

在此基础上，制定一个计划。对于你想改进的方面，定义清楚"成功是什么样子"，并列出下一步行动。这可能意味着调整某个习惯、练习某项技能，或建立新的反馈闭环。如果你不确定该如何落实这些改变，尽管去寻求支持——向同事、导师、经理，甚至 AI 助手求助。例如，你可以这样提示它："帮我制定一个每周计划，来改进这条反馈所指出的问题。"

This does not mean you have to act on every piece of feedback. The goal is to identify the insights that resonate most and create a plan of action. Just make sure to close the loop with the person who gave it, especially if they took the time to share something thoughtfully. Acknowledge their input and share why you're choosing not to act right now, whether it's due to prioritization, context, or a different perspective. Leaving feedback unaddressed without explanation can unintentionally signal that their input doesn't matter, which can discourage future feedback.

这并不意味着你必须对每一条反馈都照做。目标是识别出那些最能引起你共鸣的洞察，并制定一份行动计划。但一定要和给你反馈的人闭环，尤其是当他们花了心思认真分享之后。认可他们的意见，并说明你为什么选择暂时不行动——无论是因为优先级、上下文，还是因为视角不同。如果反馈被置之不理、又不加解释，可能会无意中传递出"你的意见不重要"的信号，从而打击他们未来继续给反馈的积极性。

After applying the feedback, it's essential to follow up. Monitor your progress on the areas you're working to improve and document what's working or what still needs adjustment. Schedule a follow-up conversation with the person who gave you the feedback to check how you're doing. An AI assistant tool can help you draft a plan for how to follow up, prepare questions, or even simulate a response to difficult feedback so you can practice. Prompt: "I received feedback that I tend to interrupt people in meetings. Can you help me come up with three questions to ask in a follow-up one-on-one and a short message to open the conversation?" This creates accountability and shows your commitment to growth.

在把反馈付诸行动之后，跟进至关重要。监控你在那些待改进方面的进展，记录下哪些奏效了、哪些仍需调整。和给你反馈的人约一次跟进谈话，看看你做得怎么样。AI 助手可以帮你草拟跟进计划、准备问题，甚至模拟一次对棘手反馈的回应让你练习。提示词可以是："我收到反馈说，我在会上容易打断别人。你能帮我想三个问题，用在跟进的一对一里，再写一小段话来开场吗？"这既建立了问责，也表明了你对成长的承诺。

— PDF p.132 —

Whether you're giving or receiving feedback, keep in mind that, as a tech lead, your actions set the tone for your team. How you handle feedback demonstrates to others how they should approach their own growth. By investing in this skill, you not only improve yourself but also create a culture that values continuous learning and development.

无论你是在给出反馈还是接收反馈，都要记住：作为技术负责人，你的行为为团队定下了基调。你如何对待反馈，就是在向别人示范他们该如何对待自己的成长。通过磨炼这项技能，你不仅提升了自己，也营造出一种重视持续学习与发展的文化。

How to Give Useful Feedback to Your Team如何向团队提供有用的反馈

Great feedback is all about balance: a mix of improvement-focused feedback and positive feedback. It's not just about pointing out where someone needs to improve or praising them when they've done well; it's about doing both consistently and with purpose. And just as trust is vital when receiving feedback, it's equally important when giving it. Trust grows when team members know you're honest with them, celebrating their strengths while also being brave enough to highlight areas for growth.

好的反馈关键在于平衡：既要有点改进导向的反馈，也要有正面反馈。它不只是指出对方哪里需要改进、或在对方做得好时表扬几句；而是要持续、有意识地两者兼顾。正如信任在接收反馈时至关重要，在给出反馈时同样不可或缺。当团队成员知道你对他们坦诚——既为他们的长处喝彩，也有勇气点出成长空间——信任就会生长。

Let's be clear: balanced feedback doesn't have to follow the "feedback sandwich" approach. Personally, I find it inefficient. Wrapping constructive feedback between two layers of praise can dilute the message and often comes across as insincere. In practice, it tends to confuse more than it helps.

需要说清楚：平衡的反馈并不一定要套用"反馈三明治"那一套。就我个人而言，我觉得它效率很低。把建设性反馈夹在两层表扬之间，会冲淡信息，而且常常显得不真诚。实际用起来，它带来的困惑往往多于帮助。

If you focus only on improvement-focused feedback, your team may begin to resent you. They might start seeing you as someone who only delivers bad news.

如果你只盯着改进导向的反馈，团队可能会开始对你心生怨气。他们可能会把你看成一个只会带来坏消息的人。

On the other hand, if you give only positive feedback, it can erode trust as well. People know they aren't perfect, and when they're not given areas to improve, your praise begins to feel insincere, or they might question your ability to observe the work they're doing. Over time, they might think, "Sure, I know I'm good at running retrospectives, but what should I work on?" Funny enough, too much positive feedback can actually hurt your credibility as a leader.

反过来，如果你只给正面反馈，同样会侵蚀信任。人人都知道自己并非完人；当没人告诉他们该改进什么时，你的表扬就开始显得虚伪，或者他们会怀疑你有没有真正在观察他们的工作。久而久之，他们可能会想："好吧，我知道我复盘开得不错，可我该在哪些方面下功夫呢？"说来有趣，过多的正面反馈，反而会损害你作为领导者的公信力。

There's no magic formula for how much positive versus improvement-focused feedback you should give; it's not about numbers or metrics. Instead, it's about developing awareness of your tendencies and trying to find a balance that works for you and your team. Do you tend to focus only on what needs to be improved? Or are you also regularly acknowledging what's going well?

至于正面反馈和改进导向反馈该各占多少比例，并没有什么神奇公式；这跟数字或指标无关。它关乎的是：觉察自己的倾向，并努力找到一种适合你和团队的平衡。你是不是往往只盯着需要改进的地方？还是说，你也会经常肯定那些做得不错的部分？

— PDF p.133 —

For example, I used to focus almost exclusively on improvement-focused feedback. I was always on the lookout for areas of improvement and didn't hesitate to share them. Then, during a performance review, the structure required me to provide positive feedback as well. The positive impact it had on my team was undeniable. I realized how much people valued hearing what they were doing well. From that moment, I started giving positive feedback more often and with the same intentionality as corrective feedback: tracking it, providing clear examples, and delivering it at the right time.

举个例子，我过去几乎只盯着改进导向的反馈。我总是在寻找可以改进的地方，并且毫不犹豫地指出来。后来有一次绩效评估，流程要求我也给出正面反馈。它给团队带来的积极影响是不可否认的。我这才意识到，大家有多么渴望听到自己哪里做得好。从那时起，我开始更频繁地给出正面反馈，并且带着和纠正性反馈同样的用心：记录它、给出清晰的例子、并在恰当的时机递出它。

If you're someone who avoids constructive feedback because you're worried about how it might be received, start small. Pick one person and practice having those conversations. On the flip side, if you find yourself primarily delivering constructive feedback, challenge yourself to throw in some encouragement or praise, even if it feels obvious. It might be as simple as saying, "Great job facilitating that retrospective. The way you handled the conflict was spot on."

如果你是那种因为担心反馈会被如何接受而回避建设性反馈的人，那就从小处着手。挑一个人，先练习和他开展这类对话。反过来，如果你发现自己主要在给建设性反馈，那就挑战自己，加进去一些鼓励或表扬——哪怕它显得再显而易见。可能就只是说一句："这次复盘你主持得很好，你处理那个冲突的方式非常到位。"

Once you experience the value of stepping outside your comfort zone, whether it's giving constructive feedback or positive feedback, you'll see the difference it makes in your team. For me, it became impossible to go back.

一旦你体会到走出舒适区的价值——无论是给出建设性反馈还是正面反馈——你就会看到它给团队带来的不同。对我而言，尝到甜头之后，就再也回不去了。

Balanced feedback also means ensuring that everyone on your team receives it equally. Avoid falling into the trap of giving all your praise to certain team members while neglecting others. Favoritism, even if unintentional, can create a toxic dynamic and make people feel undervalued.

平衡的反馈还意味着要确保团队里的每个人都能公平地接收到它。要避免掉进一个陷阱：把所有表扬都给了某些成员，却忽略了另一些人。偏心——哪怕是无心的——也会制造出一种有毒的氛围，让人感到不被重视。

In this section, I'll explore the core principles of good feedback and then dive into both positive and constructive feedback, exploring their unique challenges and incredible value when done right.

在本节中，我会先探讨良好反馈的核心原则，然后深入正面反馈和建设性反馈，分别剖析它们各自的独特挑战，以及在做对时所能带来的巨大价值。

UNDERSTANDING THE FIVE PRINCIPLES OF GOOD FEEDBACK理解良好反馈的五项原则

Most people think that useful feedback is all about telling someone how to change their behavior. In my experience, advice is just a small part of what makes feedback truly effective. Figure 5-1 shows the five key elements that make feedback useful: giving it at the right time, being as specific and clear as possible, staying honest, and making it a continuous practice. In this section, I'll break down each of these criteria, with real examples and practical tips on how to apply them effectively.

大多数人以为，有用的反馈无非就是告诉别人该如何改变自己的行为。以我的经验，建议只是让反馈真正有效的一小部分。图 5-1 展示了让反馈变得有用的五个关键要素：在恰当的时机给出、尽可能具体而清晰、保持诚实，以及把它变成一种持续的习惯。在本节中，我会逐条拆解这些标准，并配以真实的例子和实用的技巧，说明如何有效地运用它们。

— PDF p.134 —

1. Good feedback is timely1. 良好反馈及时

The value of feedback diminishes the longer you wait to give it. The more time that passes, the less relevant and impactful it becomes. Yet, many tech leads hold off, waiting for what they think is the "right moment," which often ends up being during performance reviews. But by then, feedback like "The way you handled that client conversation six months ago was great" is far too stale to make a meaningful impact.

你给出反馈拖得越久，它的价值就越低。时间隔得越久，它就越不切题、越没分量。然而，许多技术负责人迟迟不开口，等着他们心目中的"恰当时机"——而那往往最终变成了绩效评估的时候。可到那时，像"你六个月前处理那次客户沟通的方式很棒"这样的反馈，早已馊透，根本产生不了有意义的影响。

Also, delaying constructive feedback can lead to long-term consequences. Instead of addressing issues promptly, frustrations build up, and when the feedback finally comes out, it's often wrapped in passive-aggressive comments like "Should we just put Chris in charge of all meetings, since he talks the most anyway?" or blunt, hurtful remarks like "Why do you keep making the same mistake?" By this point, the problem feels bigger, harder to address, and more damaging to the relationship.

此外，拖延建设性反馈还会带来长期后果。问题没有被及时处理，不满不断积累；等反馈终于爆发出来时，往往裹着被动攻击式的措辞，比如"既然 Chris 话最多，要不所有会都让他来主持吧？"或者是粗暴伤人的话："你怎么老犯同一个错？"到这个时候，问题显得更大、更难处理，对关系的伤害也更深。

Here's a common scenario: imagine you've been silently hoping a team member will improve their code quality. Instead of addressing it early on, you drop hints in retrospectives or make vague comments like "We need to improve our testing." Months go by, and the same issues persist. Now you're forced into a difficult conversation: "Your tasks consistently come back from QA with bugs, and this has been happening for months. We need to open a performance improvement process."

来看一个常见场景：设想你一直默默盼着某位团队成员能把代码质量提上去。你没有及早指出，而是在复盘里旁敲侧击，或者说些含糊的话，比如"我们得把测试搞上去"。几个月过去，老问题依然存在。现在你被迫进行一场艰难的谈话："你提交的任务每次从 QA 回来都带着 bug，而且这种情况已经持续好几个月了。我们得启动一个绩效改进流程。"

At this point, the team member is likely shocked. "Why didn't you tell me sooner?" they'll ask, and they'd be right to. Early, clear feedback could have given them the chance to adjust their habits, avoid escalation, and regain your trust.

到这个时候，这位团队成员多半会震惊。"你为什么不早告诉我？"他们会问，而且他们问得在理。及早、清晰的反馈，本可以给他们机会去调整习惯、避免事态升级、并重新赢得你的信任。

— PDF p.135 —

I've seen team members turn things around completely once they understood the problem and felt supported in working on it. The earlier you speak up, the more manageable and less painful the issue becomes, for both of you.

我见过不少团队成员，一旦理解了问题、并感到有人支持自己去改进，情况就彻底扭转了。你开口越早，问题对你、对他们都越可控、也越不痛苦。

Don't miss the chance to give feedback when it's fresh and relevant, whether it's positive or constructive. Aim to deliver it soon after the moment occurs, ideally the same day or within a few days. If strong emotions are involved, give the situation space to settle, but don't let it slip away entirely. Acting while the context is still top of mind ensures your words have greater clarity and impact.

不要错过反馈还新鲜、还切题的那个时机，无论它是正面的还是建设性的。尽量在事情发生后尽快给出，最好当天或几天之内。如果当时情绪很激动，可以给局面一点时间冷静下来，但别让它彻底溜走。在背景还历历在目时行动，能确保你的话更清晰、更有分量。

2. Good feedback is specific2. 良好反馈具体

The more specific your feedback, the more useful it becomes. Specific feedback gives people a clear direction for improvement and provides tangible points to address. It focuses on facts, which reduces the chance of defensive reactions and shifts the conversation toward solutions rather than debates.

你的反馈越具体，它就越有用。具体的反馈给人指明了改进的清晰方向，并提供了可以着手的实打实地带。它聚焦于事实，从而降低了对方产生防御反应的可能，把对话引向解决方案，而不是争论不休。

Let's take a common situation: addressing code quality with a team member. A vague comment like "Your code is full of bugs" might seem like feedback, but it's far from effective. Instead of leading to improvement, it's likely to trigger defensiveness. The other person might respond with "That's not true; most of my code passes QA," and they'd have a valid point if you're referring only to their latest task. Without specifics, they're left in the dark about what you actually mean.

举个常见的情形：和团队成员谈代码质量。一句含糊的"你的代码全是 bug"看似是反馈，实则远远谈不上有效。它非但不能带来改进，反而很可能激起防御。对方可能会回你："那不是真的，我大部分代码都能通过 QA。"如果你指的只是他最近这一个任务，他这话其实站得住脚。没有具体细节，他完全摸不清你到底在说什么。

Now imagine instead saying, "The task you finished yesterday had missing tests and bugs that were caught in QA." This shifts the focus to facts that are hard to challenge, making it clear which task you're talking about. It opens the door for the other person to explain what happened. Perhaps they were overwhelmed, or it was a type of task they hadn't handled before. Whatever the case, being specific transforms the conversation into a productive discussion about solutions rather than a defensive argument about their overall performance.

现在换个说法试试："你昨天完成的那个任务，缺了测试，而且有几个 bug 被 QA 揪了出来。"这就把焦点移到了难以反驳的事实上，也清楚地点明了你说的是哪个任务。这为对方解释情况打开了门。也许当时他忙得焦头烂额，或者那是一种他从没处理过的任务类型。无论如何，具体性能把对话变成一场关于解决方案的富有成效的讨论，而不是一场就他整体表现展开的防御性争论。

Specificity also makes feedback fairer. In performance reviews or promotion discussions, vague generalizations can introduce implicit bias or lead to unfair evaluations. By grounding your feedback in clear, recent, observable examples, you create a more objective and equitable foundation for assessing performance. It ensures that everyone is evaluated based on what they've actually done, not assumptions, impressions, or stereotypes.

具体还能让反馈更公平。在绩效评估或晋升讨论中，含糊的一概而论会引入隐性偏见，或导致不公平的评判。把你的反馈建立在清晰、新近、可观察的例子之上，你就为评估表现打下了一个更客观、更公正的基础。它确保每个人都是基于自己实际做过的事被评价，而不是基于假设、印象或刻板印象。

A general rule: be specific. Never assume people know what you're referring to; it's better to repeat yourself than leave them guessing.

一条通则：要具体。永远不要想当然地认为别人知道你在说什么；与其让他们猜，不如你自己多重复一遍。

— PDF p.136 —

3. Good feedback is clear3. 良好反馈清晰

Good feedback is not just about what you say; it's about how you say it. Even if your message is specific, it can still fall flat if it's buried under vague or hesitant phrasing. Clear feedback means expressing your message directly, without hedging, downplaying, or confusing the core point.

好的反馈不只是关于你说什么，还关于你怎么说。即便你的信息很具体，如果它被含糊、犹豫的措辞所埋没，依然会落空。清晰的反馈，意味着直接表达你的意思，不闪烁其词、不淡化、也不让核心观点变得模糊。

Let's consider an example. Instead of saying, "I think you might have said the wrong thing this morning, and I think it might have happened last week too…maybe it was a misunderstanding?," opt for something direct: "This morning in standup, you said we have to integrate three services, but we need to integrate only two. I was concerned because I had shared the correct information with everyone yesterday, and it may have caused some confusion." The second version leaves no room for ambiguity; it pinpoints the issue, explains the impact, and sets the stage for a constructive conversation.

来看个例子。与其说："我觉得你今天早上可能说错话了，而且我觉得上周好像也发生过一次……也许是个误会？"不如选择一种直接的说法："今天早上站会上，你说我们要集成三个服务，但其实我们只需要集成两个。我有点担心，因为昨天我已经把正确的信息发给大家了，这可能造成了一些困惑。"第二个版本不留任何模糊的余地；它精准地点出问题、解释影响，并为一场建设性对话铺好了路。

Avoid vague qualifiers like "maybe," "I think," or "sort of." They dilute your message and make it easier to ignore.

避免用"也许""我觉得""有点儿"这类含糊的修饰词。它们会冲淡你的信息，让它更容易被忽略。

4. Good feedback is honest4. 良好反馈诚实

Insincere compliments can do more harm than good. If you have nothing constructive or genuine to say, don't force yourself to come up with something. People can tell when feedback isn't sincere, and it makes people trust you less.

不真诚的恭维往往弊大于利。如果你没有任何建设性或真心想讲的话，就别硬挤出来。人们能闻出反馈里的不真诚，而那会让他们更不信任你。

When giving feedback, focus on being kind, not just nice. Nice might mean telling a developer "Great job on the feature!" when you know the code wasn't up to the team's usual standards. Being kind means acknowledging their effort but addressing the issue honestly: "I appreciate the effort you put into delivering this feature quickly. However, the implementation could use some improvement, especially in terms of readability and edge case handling. Let's sit down and go through it together."

给出反馈时，要力求"善意"，而不只是"客气"。客气可能意味着：明知代码没达到团队一贯水准，却还是对开发说"这个功能做得真棒！"而善意，则是既认可他们的付出、又诚实地指出问题："我很欣赏你为快速交付这个功能所付出的努力。不过，这个实现还有改进空间，尤其是在可读性和边界情况处理上。我们坐下来一起过一遍吧。"

Kindness encourages growth and respect, while superficial praise only delays improvement and undermines credibility.

善意能促进成长与尊重，而浮于表面的表扬只会拖延改进、损害公信力。

5. Good feedback is continuous5. 良好反馈持续

Feedback doesn't end when you give it. Tracking it is how you make it stick and see its impact.

反馈不会在你递出去的那一刻就结束。持续跟踪它，才能让它真正扎根、并看到它的影响。

Create individual notes for each member, jotting down the feedback you've given, the date, and any examples of progress or patterns that keep showing up.

为每位成员单独建一份记录，草草记下你给过的反馈、日期，以及那些反复出现的进步事例或行为模式。

Follow-up is where the magic happens. If the behavior improves, acknowledge it. Positive reinforcement goes a long way. If it doesn't, don't just let it slide. Bring it up again with clear examples, and work together on the next steps. The intention is making sure it actually leads to real, lasting change.

跟进才是魔法发生的地方。如果行为改善了，就予以认可。正面强化的作用非常大。如果没有改善，也不要就此放过。带着清晰的例子再提一次，并和对方一起商定下一步。目的在于确保反馈真正带来切实、持久的改变。

— PDF p.137 —

Mastering these five principles, timely, specific, clear, honest, and continuous, is what turns feedback from a vague suggestion into a meaningful catalyst for growth. Whether you're praising a team member or helping them course-correct, these principles ensure your message lands with clarity and purpose.

掌握这五项原则——及时、具体、清晰、诚实、持续——才能把反馈从一句含糊的建议，变成一股有意义的成长催化剂。无论你是在表扬一位团队成员，还是在帮他纠正方向，这些原则都能确保你的信息带着清晰的意图、真正落到对方心里。

HOW TO GIVE POSITIVE FEEDBACK如何给出正面反馈

Most tech leads don't give enough positive feedback because they assume it's obvious. Saying things like "That was an awesome presentation, very clear and to the point," "I really liked how you handled that conversation," or even a simple, "I really appreciate you jumping in to help Ana with that bug yesterday" just doesn't come naturally. Tech leads often think, "They already know they're good at that" or "Someone else must have told them," completely underestimating the value of these words. But what if that "someone else" is thinking the same thing? Unlike improvement-focused feedback, which highlights areas for growth, positive feedback reinforces what's working well and motivates people to keep doing it.

大多数技术负责人给出的正面反馈都不够，因为他们觉得这不是明摆着的吗。像"刚才的汇报太棒了，非常清晰、切中要点""我很欣赏你处理那次谈话的方式"，甚至一句简单的"昨天你主动帮 Ana 排查那个 bug，我真的很感激"——这些话就是说不出口。技术负责人常常想："他们自己肯定知道自己在这方面很行"或者"肯定已经有人告诉他们了"，完全低估了这些话的价值。可万一那个"别人"也在想同样的事呢？改进导向的反馈指出成长空间，而正面反馈则强化那些做得好的地方，激励人们继续保持。

A lot of people associate feedback only with criticism or corrective feedback, assuming positive feedback isn't necessary. Meanwhile, the techies I work with often tell me how much they crave their tech lead's acknowledgment, but they rarely get it. Positive feedback seems to show up only when something huge happens like finishing a project early, during a retro, when going above and beyond or staying late to fix an incident. And even then, it's often just a quick "Great job."

很多人把反馈只和批评或纠正性反馈划等号，认为正面反馈没什么必要。可与此同时，和我共事的技术人常常告诉我，他们有多么渴望技术负责人的认可，却又很少得到。正面反馈似乎只在大事发生时才冒出来——比如提前完成一个项目、在复盘里、有人表现突出、或者熬夜修线上故障。即便到了那个时候，往往也只是一句匆匆的"干得漂亮"。

People need encouragement to stay motivated. They need proof they're heading in the right direction. Positive feedback is your chance to provide that, and it's just as important as constructive feedback. Genuine appreciation strengthens relationships: people feel more connected to those who recognize their efforts.

人需要鼓励才能保持动力。他们需要证据，证明自己走在正确的方向上。正面反馈就是你提供这份证据的机会，它和建设性反馈同样重要。真诚的赏识能巩固关系：人们会和那些认可自己付出的人产生更深的联结。

And positivity is contagious: when someone feels seen and valued, it lifts their mood and often spreads to others. A team that regularly celebrates wins, big or small, tends to be more engaged, collaborative, and resilient. It can be as simple as adding a kudos column to your retrospective board where team members can recognize each other's contributions. The emotional impact of positive feedback directly affects how people show up at work.

而且积极情绪是会传染的：当一个人感到被看见、被重视时，他的心情会变好，还往往会感染其他人。一支经常庆祝胜利（无论大小）的团队，往往更投入、更协作、也更有韧性。这事可以简单到：在你的复盘看板上加一个"点赞"栏，让团队成员互相认可彼此的贡献。正面反馈带来的情绪影响，会直接作用于人们在工作中的状态。

The key is to treat it with the same level of effort and intentionality. Apply the same five principles I introduced earlier in the chapter to positive feedback, and you'll see the difference it makes:

关键在于，要用同等的用心和诚意来对待它。把我在本章前面介绍的那五项原则，同样应用到正面反馈上，你就会看到它带来的不同：

— PDF p.138 —

Timely及时

Positive feedback is most valuable when it's given as soon as possible. Don't wait six months to mention something great they did during a performance review. A simple "Awesome presentation today" or "I really appreciated how you handled that situation yesterday" during a one-on-one can have a massive impact.

正面反馈在尽快给出时最有价值。不要等六个月后、到绩效评估时才提起他们做过的某件好事。在一次一对一里，一句简单的"今天汇报很棒"或"我很欣赏你昨天处理那件事的方式"，就能产生巨大的影响。

It doesn't even have to be a formal conversation. Imagine someone nails a presentation. Send them a Slack message: "Loved how you presented the strategy using those visual diagrams. Great job showcasing the impact of our work!" A short, timely comment like this can make a big difference.

它甚至不必是一次正式谈话。设想某人刚漂亮地做完一次汇报。给他发一条 Slack 消息："很喜欢你用那些可视化图表来讲这套策略。把我们工作的影响展示得真棒！"这样一句简短而及时的话，就能带来很大的不同。

Specific具体

Vague praise like "You communicate well" is nice, but it doesn't help someone understand their strengths. Instead, pinpoint exactly what you appreciated: "The way you handled that tough conversation with the client the other day was impressive. Staying calm and finding a solution they agreed to really stood out." Specific feedback not only helps them see their strengths but also shows that you're paying attention.

像"你沟通得很好"这种含糊的表扬，听着是舒服，但并不能帮对方认清自己的长处。相反，要点明你究竟欣赏什么："前几天你和客户那场艰难谈话的处理方式令人印象深刻。你保持冷静、并找到一个他们都能接受的方案，这一点特别突出。"具体的反馈不仅帮他们看清自己的优势，也向他们表明你一直在用心观察。

Clear清晰

Clarity adds weight to your feedback. Instead of saying, "I feel like you're ready to lead this initiative," connect it to specific examples: "The way you handled this task, dealing with dependencies, aligning the team on strategy, and delivering on time, shows you're the perfect fit to take over this initiative." Clear feedback leaves no room for doubt and boosts their confidence in taking on new challenges.

清晰会为你的反馈增加分量。与其说"我觉得你已经可以牵头这件事了"，不如把它和具体例子联系起来："你处理这个任务的方式——应对依赖、在策略上对齐团队、并按时交付——说明你正好适合接手这个项目。"清晰的反馈不留任何怀疑的余地，也会提升他们迎接新挑战的信心。

Honest诚实

More positive feedback doesn't mean you should force it or say things you don't believe. If you don't genuinely have something good to say, don't say anything at all. People can see right through insincere compliments, and it will damage your credibility.

更多的正面反馈，并不意味着你该硬挤出来、或说些自己都不信的话。如果你心里确实没有什么好说的，那就什么都别说。人们一眼就能看穿不真诚的恭维，而那会损害你的公信力。

That said, if you put effort into noticing what people are doing, I am sure you'll find plenty of opportunities to praise them authentically. Everyone has things to be praised about also.

话虽如此，只要你用心去留意人们在做什么，我相信你一定会发现大量可以真诚表扬的机会。每个人都有值得被表扬的地方。

— PDF p.139 —

Praising effort, not just results, is also a powerful strategy, especially for team members who may not be the highest performers yet but are putting in real work to grow. Recognizing behaviors like perseverance, initiative, or thoughtful collaboration can reinforce those habits and keep people motivated. For example: "I really appreciate the time you've been investing in understanding the new system. It's clear you're putting in the effort to improve."

表扬努力、而不只是结果，也是一种强有力的策略，尤其对那些目前还不是最高绩效、但正在为成长付出真实努力的团队成员。认可他们身上的毅力、主动性或周到的协作等行为，能强化这些习惯、让人保持动力。例如："我很欣赏你一直在花时间钻研这套新系统。看得出来你在为提升自己下功夫。"

Continuous持续

Giving positive feedback isn't a one-and-done thing. Just like constructive feedback, you need to track it and reinforce it over time. If someone consistently demonstrates a skill you've praised, let them know you're noticing their growth: "You've been so consistent with your communication skills lately. It's making a big difference in how the team collaborates."

给出正面反馈不是一锤子买卖。和建设性反馈一样，你需要记录它、并随时间不断强化它。如果有人持续展现出你曾表扬过的某项技能，就让他们知道你注意到了他们的成长："你最近在沟通上一直这么稳。这对团队的协作方式产生了很大的积极影响。"

Even when applying these principles, many people struggle to come up with the right words for positive feedback. Here are a few examples to help you get started:

即便用上了这些原则，很多人还是苦于想不出正面反馈该怎么措辞。下面给几个例子帮你入门：

  • I really appreciate how you structured that proposal; it was so clear and actionable.我很欣赏你把那份提案的结构安排得这么好；非常清晰、可落地。
  • Thanks for stepping in during the incident yesterday. You kept things calm and organized.谢谢你昨天在故障时顶上。你让一切保持冷静、井然有序。
  • Pairing with the new joiners over the past two weeks has really helped them get up to speed quickly.过去两周你和新人结对，真的帮他们很快上手了。
  • Your documentation for the new process saved me so much time; thank you for putting that together.你为新流程写的文档帮我省了超多时间；谢谢你整理出来。
  • You've been doing a fantastic job leading standups; everyone's much more aligned lately.你主持站会一直特别棒；最近大家对齐多了。
  • You consistently notice edge cases that others miss; it's a huge asset to our team's quality.你总能注意到别人漏掉的边界情况；这对我们团队的质量来说是一大法宝。

Keep in mind that how you deliver positive feedback matters too. While public praise can be a great motivator, in some cases it may unintentionally create discomfort or perceptions of favoritism. Some people simply prefer to receive recognition in private. Take a moment to consider the individual and the context: what's motivating for one person might feel awkward or alienating to another. When in doubt, tailor your message to what will land best with that person.

请记住，你怎么递出正面反馈同样重要。公开表扬固然是很好的激励，但在某些情况下，它可能无意中让人不适，或让人觉得你偏心。有些人就是更喜欢私下接受认可。花点时间想想对方这个人、以及当时的情境：对一个人有激励作用的做法，对另一个人可能让他尴尬或疏远。拿不准的时候，就把你的话调整到最适合这个人的方式。

Positive feedback is one of the simplest, most effective tools you have as a tech lead to build motivation, confidence, and trust on your team. It doesn't require a big gesture, just your attention and intention. Make it a habit. The more you practice noticing and acknowledging what's working, the more your team will feel seen, supported, and empowered to keep improving.

正面反馈，是你作为技术负责人用来在团队中建立动力、信心和信任的最简单、也最有效的工具之一。它不需要什么大动作，只需要你的关注和用心。把它变成一种习惯。你越是练习去留意、去肯定那些做得好的地方，团队就越会感到被看见、被支持，并被激发出持续改进的力量。

— PDF p.140 —

HOW TO GIVE CONSTRUCTIVE FEEDBACK如何给出建设性反馈

There's a natural hesitation that comes with giving constructive feedback. Just like team members might avoid giving feedback to their tech lead for fear of repercussions, tech leads often fear how their team members will react. You might worry about hurting someone's feelings or damaging the relationship. And that's not something to dismiss. How you deliver the feedback matters just as much as what you say. If handled poorly, even well-intentioned feedback can cause defensiveness or resentment.

给出建设性反馈时，人天生会有些犹豫。就像团队成员可能因为怕有后果而不敢给技术负责人提反馈一样，技术负责人也常常害怕团队成员会作何反应。你可能会担心伤了对方的感情、或破坏彼此的关系。而这种顾虑是不该被轻视的。你怎么递出反馈，和你说什么同样重要。如果处理不当，即便出于好意的反馈，也可能引起防御或怨恨。

But avoiding the conversation isn't the solution, especially when the behavior is repeated. It only makes the problem bigger.

但回避这场对话并不是办法，尤其是当这种行为反复出现时。回避只会让问题变得更大。

I once had a team member who consistently dismissed suggestions unless they came from her. Every time someone proposed a new idea, her first reaction was to poke holes in it, trying to find the flaw, the risk, the reason it wouldn't work. The rest of the team noticed, but our tech lead at the time said nothing. Over time, people stopped speaking up in discussions. They didn't want to risk being shut down, myself included.

我曾有过一位团队成员，凡是建议只要不是她自己提的，她一概否定。每次有人提出新想法，她的第一反应就是挑刺，拼命找漏洞、找风险、找它行不通的理由。团队其他人都看在眼里，但我们当时的技术负责人什么也没说。久而久之，大家在讨论中不再发言。谁也不想冒着被怼回去的风险，我自己也一样。

Culture is not what we say. It's what we normalize. And in that silence, we normalized a culture where ideas weren't safe. By not saying anything, the tech lead unintentionally reinforced the behavior, and the damage spread.

文化不是我们嘴上说的那一套，而是我们所默许的那一套。在那片沉默中，我们默许了一种"提出想法并不安全"的文化。由于什么都不说，技术负责人无意中强化了那种行为，而损害也随之蔓延开来。

A lot of tech leads use "I am too busy" as a reason to postpone tough feedback. But waiting doesn't save time; it creates more work. In this case, what could've been one honest conversation early on turned into several. The longer you delay, the more relationships are affected, and the harder it becomes to untangle the mess.

很多技术负责人拿"我太忙"当借口，把棘手的反馈一拖再拖。但等待并不节省时间；它只会制造更多的工作量。在上面这个例子里，本可以早一点用一次坦诚的谈话解决的事，最后变成了好几次。你拖得越久，受到影响的关系就越多，那团乱麻也就越难解开。

Some feedback cannot even wait until after. Sometimes, especially when incorrect information affects the direction of the conversation, you need to step in right away.

有些反馈甚至等不到"事后"。有时候，尤其是当错误信息正在把讨论带偏时，你需要当场就介入。

Let's say someone shares an outdated diagram during a client meeting, and the discussion continues based on incorrect assumptions. In those cases, it's better to gently interrupt: "Actually, it looks like this diagram is outdated. We've made a few changes since it was created. Let me pull up the latest version" or "We might need to revisit this once we've updated it."

设想在一次客户会议上，有人展示了一张过时的图，而讨论正基于错误的假设继续下去。在这种情况下，最好是温和地打断："其实，这张图看起来已经过时了。自它绘制以来我们做了几处改动。我把最新版调出来。"或者"等我们更新之后，可能需要再回头讨论一下这个。"

It's a tricky balance, because while you don't want to embarrass anyone in the moment, you also have a responsibility to protect the integrity of the discussion. In situations like these, it's OK to step in to correct the information, especially when the conversation depends on it. What matters just as much is what you do after: follow up with the person privately. Check in on how they felt about you jumping in, and discuss how you can handle similar situations together in the future.

这是一种微妙的平衡：你既不想当场让谁难堪，又有责任维护讨论的严肃性。在这类情形下，站出来纠正信息是可以的，尤其是当整场讨论都依赖它的时候。同样重要的是你之后怎么做：私下找那个人跟进。问问他们对你当场介入有什么感受，并一起讨论今后遇到类似情况该如何处理。

— PDF p.141 —

Addressing issues quickly keeps them from snowballing into bigger problems. It also shows your team that you're paying attention and that you care enough to address issues directly.

迅速处理问题，能防止它们像滚雪球一样越滚越大。这也向团队表明：你一直在留意，而且你足够在乎、愿意直面问题。

I'll go over some strategies that can make delivering constructive feedback easier.

下面我会介绍一些策略，让给出建设性反馈这件事变得更容易。

Start with the five principles of good feedback we covered earlier: timely, specific, clear, honest, and continuous. If you keep these in mind, you're already ahead of most.

从我们前面讲过的良好反馈五原则入手：及时、具体、清晰、诚实、持续。只要把这几条记在心里，你就已经超过大多数人了。

Adapt your style to the individual. Understanding the person you're giving feedback to is just as important as the content of the feedback itself. Each team member is different, and every new joiner brings a unique dynamic. Some may prefer directness; others may need more context or time to process. Pay attention to their communication style, personality, and experience level, and adjust your approach accordingly. You can even ask them how they prefer to receive feedback or which style they prefer.

让你的方式因人而异。理解你反馈的对象，和反馈内容本身同样重要。每位团队成员都不一样，每个新人都会带来独特的互动氛围。有人更喜欢直接；有人则需要更多背景或时间来消化。留意他们的沟通风格、性格和经验水平，并据此调整你的方式。你甚至可以直接问他们：希望以怎样的方式接收反馈、更喜欢哪种风格。

Another strategy I've found invaluable comes from Nonviolent Communication, discussed in the section "Communicate Effectively" on page 63: focus on your own feelings. It's surprisingly effective, and underused. Usually, as adults, we are not encouraged to talk about how we feel, especially at work. I come from a culture where discussing emotions isn't really the norm. But once I saw how it shifted the tone of difficult conversations, both for me and the other person, I couldn't stop using it.

另一个我觉得极为宝贵的策略，来自"非暴力沟通"（见第 63 页"有效沟通"一节）：聚焦于你自己的感受。它的效果好得出奇，却被严重低估。通常，作为成年人，我们并不被鼓励谈论自己的感受，尤其是在工作场合。我来自一种不太习惯谈论情绪的文化。但一旦我看到它如何转变了艰难对话的基调——对我、对对方都是——我就再也停不下来用它了。

Saying something like "I felt dismissed when you jumped in over me in this morning's meeting while I was explaining how the system works" makes it hard to argue. If they respond with "I didn't mean to" or "It was just a misunderstanding," bring the focus back gently: "I understand it wasn't intentional, but that's how it landed for me," so they're aware of the actual impact of their actions.

说一句类似这样的话："今天早上的会上，我正在讲解系统是怎么运作的，你插话盖过了我，当时我觉得自己被无视了。"——这种话让人很难反驳。如果对方回应"我不是故意的"或"只是个误会"，就温和地把焦点拉回来："我理解你不是有意的，但我当时的感受就是这样。"好让他们意识到自己行为的真实影响。

Using a format to structure your message can have a big impact. It helps you stay focused, reduces emotional ambiguity, and makes your feedback easier to hear. AI assistants can support you here by offering different mental models or frameworks, like COIN or SBI. You can ask them to explain each model, compare their pros and cons, or help you choose the one that best fits your situation.

用一个固定格式来组织你的信息，会产生很大的效果。它帮你保持聚焦、减少情绪上的模糊，也让你的反馈更容易被听进去。AI 助手可以在这方面帮你：提供不同的思维模型或框架，比如 COIN 或 SBI。你可以让它解释每个模型、比较各自的优缺点，或帮你选出最适合当前情形的那一个。

— PDF p.142 —

Let's say you're working through a tough moment or trying to clarify your thoughts before a conversation. You might prompt an AI assistant with "Here's what I want to say. Can you help me express it using the SBI framework?"

假设你正在应对一个棘手的时刻，或者想在一次谈话之前理清思路。你可以这样提示 AI 助手："这是我想说的话。你能帮我用 SBI 框架把它表达出来吗？"

SBI is one of the most practical and widely used approaches for giving clear, actionable feedback.

SBI 是给出清晰、可落地反馈时最实用、也最广为使用的方法之一。

The SBI model was originally developed by the Center for Creative Leadership, and it stands for Situation–Behavior–Impact. This method helps keep feedback grounded in facts, making it easier for the recipient to hear and reducing the likelihood of defensiveness.

SBI 模型最早由创新领导力中心（Center for Creative Leadership）提出，它代表的是"情境—行为—影响"（Situation–Behavior–Impact）。这个方法有助于让反馈牢牢扎根于事实，让接收者更容易听进去，也降低了产生防御的可能。

Here is how the SBI model works:

SBI 模型是这样运作的：

Start with the situation从情境开始

Describe the specific context where the behavior occurred. Be precise about when and where it happened and who was involved. This clarity ensures the recipient understands exactly what you're referring to.

描述该行为发生时的具体背景。要说清楚是在何时、何地、有谁在场。这种清晰能确保接收者准确理解你指的是哪件事。

Move to the behavior接着说行为

Explain what the person did, focusing only on observable actions. What exactly happened? Avoid making assumptions about intentions or motivations; stick to what you saw or heard.

解释这个人具体做了什么，只聚焦于可观察到的行为。到底发生了什么？不要对其意图或动机做假设；只讲你看到或听到的。

Finish with the impact最后讲影响

Share how the behavior affected you, the team, or the work. How did this impact you personally (what you thought and/or felt)? How did it affect the team, project, or organization (e.g., confusion, delays, morale)? Be clear and specific about why this matters.

分享这个行为如何影响了你、团队或工作。它对你个人造成了怎样的影响（你当时怎么想、有什么感受）？它又如何影响了团队、项目或组织（比如造成困惑、延误、士气低落）？要清楚而具体地说明这件事为什么重要。

Let's take as an example one of the hardest scenarios for tech leads: addressing a senior developer's negative behavior. Imagine a senior team member constantly interrupts others in meetings or dismisses their ideas. Over time, the team disengages, feeling undervalued and unmotivated. This situation is challenging because the senior developer might not realize the impact of their actions. You might also hesitate to address it, either out of fear of damaging the relationship or because their expertise makes it feel like you're questioning their authority.

我们以技术负责人最棘手的情形之一为例：指出一位资深开发的负面行为。设想一位资深团队成员在会上总爱打断别人、或否定别人的想法。久而久之，团队不再投入，感到不被重视、也提不起劲。这种情况之所以难，是因为这位资深开发可能根本没意识到自己行为的影响。你也可能犹豫要不要提——要么怕破坏关系，要么因为对方资历深厚，让你觉得像是在质疑他的权威。

— PDF p.143 —

Using the SBI model, you can structure your feedback like this: "During yesterday's planning meeting, I observed that you interrupted several team members when they were sharing their thoughts. This made me uncomfortable because it affected the flow of the discussion. I also noticed that after each interruption, some team members seemed less engaged and hesitant to contribute further."

运用 SBI 模型，你可以把反馈组织成这样："在昨天的计划会上，我注意到你打断了好几位正在分享想法的团队成员。这让我有些不安，因为它影响了讨论的流畅性。我还注意到，每次被打断之后，有些成员似乎就更不投入、也更不愿再发言了。"

This kind of feedback is clear, fact-based, and leaves space for the person receiving the feedback to reflect and respond constructively.

这种反馈清晰、基于事实，并给接收者留出了反思和建设性回应的空间。

This message can be broken down using the SBI model, mapped onto the situation, behavior, and impact, as follows:

这段话可以用 SBI 模型拆解，对应到情境、行为、影响三部分，如下：

Situation情境

During yesterday's planning meeting…

在昨天的计划会上……

Behavior行为

I observed that you interrupted several team members while they were sharing their thoughts.

我注意到你打断了好几位正在分享想法的团队成员。

Impact影响

This made me uncomfortable because it affected the flow of the discussion. I also noticed that after each interruption, some team members seemed less engaged and hesitant to contribute further.

这让我有些不安，因为它影响了讨论的流畅性。我还注意到，每次被打断之后，有些成员似乎就更不投入、也更不愿再发言了。

Once you've delivered the feedback, give the person time to process it. Not everyone can immediately dive into next steps. Pay attention to their reaction and decide whether to continue the conversation now or follow up later.

一旦递出了反馈，给对方时间去消化。不是每个人都能立刻进入"下一步"的。留意他们的反应，再决定是现在继续谈，还是之后再跟进。

When you're ready to move forward, shift the focus to understanding the reasoning behind the behavior. Was it intentional? A misunderstanding? Or is there an external factor affecting their performance? Use a coaching approach to help them identify solutions. Ask open-ended questions like "How do you think we can address this?" or "What steps do you think would help?" People are more likely to commit to a plan if the ideas come from them. Only step in with suggestions if they ask for your advice, and even then, let them choose the option that feels most achievable to them.

当你准备好往下走时，把焦点转到理解行为背后的原因上。是有意为之？一场误会？还是有某个外部因素在影响他们的表现？用教练式的方法，帮他们自己找出解决方案。问一些开放式问题，比如"你觉得我们该怎么解决这件事？"或"你觉得哪些步骤会有帮助？"如果主意是他们自己想出来的，他们更有可能真正投入去执行。只有在他们主动征求建议时，你才介入给出方案；即便那时，也让他们自己选那个对他们来说最可行的选项。

By delivering feedback promptly, focusing on one topic at a time, and structuring it with tools like the SBI model, you create a constructive environment for growth. It makes the feedback more digestible for the receiver and reduces the chances of defensiveness.

通过及时给出反馈、每次只聚焦一个话题、并用 SBI 模型这类工具来组织，你就为成长营造了一个建设性的环境。这让接收者更容易消化反馈，也降低了产生防御的可能。

When it comes to constructive feedback, delivering it once isn't enough. Feedback is only as effective as the follow-up that ensures it's addressed and acted upon. After you've had the initial conversation, your work isn't over. You need to track how the situation develops, observe changes in behavior, and decide whether the feedback needs to be reinforced or adjusted.

说到建设性反馈，给一次是远远不够的。反馈的效果，取决于后续有没有确保它被正视、被落实。在最初那次谈话之后，你的工作还没完。你需要跟踪事态如何发展、观察行为上的变化，并决定这条反馈是需要再强化、还是需要调整。

— PDF p.144 —

The simplest way to ensure you're following up effectively is to track the feedback you give. Create a system, like an online note for each team member, where you record what feedback you delivered, when you delivered it, any specific examples discussed, a timestamp, the actions you agreed on, and what has happened since. This serves as a record you can revisit over time, helping you see if progress has been made or if patterns persist. Make sure to store this information somewhere private and secure.

确保自己有效跟进的最简单方法，就是把你给出的反馈记录下来。建立一个系统——比如为每位团队成员建一份在线笔记——在里面记下：你给了什么反馈、什么时候给的、讨论过哪些具体例子、时间戳、双方商定的行动，以及此后发生了什么。它就是一份你可以随时翻阅的记录，帮你看清是取得了进展，还是老毛病依旧。一定要把这些信息存放在私密、安全的地方。

For example, if you've addressed issues with late arrivals to standups, track their attendance over the next few weeks. Did the feedback lead to improved punctuality, or are there still recurring issues? Adding specific examples, such as "Arrived on time for every standup this sprint" or "Late three times this week," allows you to keep the discussion grounded in facts during any follow-up conversations.

例如，如果你已经就"站会迟到"的问题沟通过，就在接下来几周里跟踪他们的出勤情况。反馈带来了守时的改善吗？还是老问题依然反复出现？加上具体的例子，比如"这个迭代每次站会都准时到"或"这周迟到了三次"，能让你在任何跟进谈话中都把讨论牢牢锚定在事实上。

Likewise, if the conversation was about code review engagement, you might note: "Reviewed 5 PRs this sprint and left constructive comments on each." Or if the topic was about responsiveness in tickets: "Replied to support queries within 24 hours consistently."

同样，如果谈的是代码评审的投入度，你可以记："这个评审了 5 个 PR，每个都留了建设性意见。"或者如果话题是工单响应速度："始终在 24 小时内回复支持类咨询。"

Regardless of the outcome, following up is mandatory to ensure your feedback is not being ignored and is being acted on. If the behavior improves, use positive reinforcing feedback to acknowledge the progress. For example, you could say, "I noticed you've been consistently on time for standups this sprint. I really appreciate the effort you've put into this. It makes a big difference for the team." Recognizing their efforts reinforces the desired behavior and motivates them to continue.

无论结果如何，跟进都是必须的，目的是确保你的反馈没有被忽视、也正在被落实。如果行为改善了，就用正面强化的反馈来认可这份进步。例如你可以说："我注意到这个迭代你站会一直很准时。我很欣赏你在这上面付出的努力。这对团队帮助很大。"认可他们的付出，能强化期望中的行为，并激励他们继续保持。

If the behavior hasn't improved, it's time to revisit the feedback using specific examples to re-address the issue. Here's where the tracking comes in handy. For instance, "I noticed you were still late three times this week. Let's discuss what didn't work and what worked since our last conversation." By tying the follow-up to observable patterns, you make it clear that the feedback is ongoing, not a one-time event.

如果行为没有改善，就该带着具体例子重提这条反馈、再次处理这个问题了。这时，你之前的记录就派上了用场。例如："我注意到你这周还是迟到了三次。我们来聊聊，自从上次谈话之后，哪些做法没奏效、哪些奏效了。"通过把跟进和可观察到的规律挂钩，你就清楚地表明了：反馈是一个持续的过程，而不是一次性事件。

Feedback isn't a one-and-done process. As you track and follow up, continue to adjust your approach as needed. If the same issue persists, consider exploring deeper reasons behind the behavior. Is there an external factor affecting their ability to change? Are they unclear on the expectations? Or do they need additional support to succeed? Asking questions and revisiting the conversation helps ensure they understand the importance of the feedback and have the tools to address it.

反馈不是一锤子买卖的过程。在你跟踪和跟进的同时，要根据需要持续调整自己的方式。如果同一个问题依然存在，就要去探究行为背后更深层的原因。是不是有某个外部因素在妨碍他们做出改变？是不是他们对预期还不清楚？又或者，他们是否需要额外的支持才能成功？通过提问、并重访这场对话，能确保他们理解这条反馈的重要性，并具备处理它所需的工具。

— PDF p.145 —

On the other hand, if the behavior improves and becomes consistent, you can begin to phase out the need for follow-ups, focusing instead on recognizing and reinforcing their strengths. The ultimate goal is to create a culture where feedback leads to growth, not just temporary fixes.

反过来，如果行为改善并趋于稳定，你就可以逐步减少跟进的频率，转而把精力放在认可和强化他们的优势上。最终目标，是营造一种让反馈导向成长、而不只是临时修补的文化。

Constructive feedback only achieves its purpose when it's followed through. Without tracking and follow-up, you risk creating confusion or leaving unresolved issues. Following up demonstrates that you're invested in their growth and that the feedback wasn't just a passing comment but a shared commitment to improvement.

建设性反馈只有在被贯彻到底时，才能实现它的目的。没有跟踪和跟进，你就可能造成困惑、或留下悬而未决的问题。跟进表明了你对他们成长的投入，也表明那条反馈不是随口一说，而是一份共同致力于改进的承诺。

Overcoming Common Challenges克服常见挑战

Even with a solid understanding of how to ask for feedback, deliver constructive feedback, and apply feedback principles effectively, challenges will still appear.

即便你已经扎实地掌握了如何请求反馈、如何给出建设性反馈、如何有效运用反馈原则，挑战依然会出现。

Tech leads often find themselves facing recurring issues like running out of feedback to give, struggling to get their team to provide honest and constructive input, or building a feedback culture within the team. These are normal pain points you will encounter in the process of feedback.

技术负责人常常会反复遇到一些难题：比如想不出还能给什么反馈、难以让团队给出诚实而建设性的意见、或是难以在团队里建立起反馈文化。这些都是你在反馈之路上必然会遇到的常见痛点。

Each of these challenges requires its own strategies to address. In the following sections, I'll break them down one by one and share practical, actionable approaches to help you navigate these tricky situations.

每一种挑战都需要各自的策略来应对。在接下来的几节里，我会逐一拆解它们，并分享务实、可落地的方法，帮你驾驭这些棘手的局面。

"I HAVE NO FEEDBACK TO GIVE""我没什么反馈可给"

Every single day offers opportunities for feedback; you just have to pay attention. Once you become intentional about looking for it, you'll start noticing things. The truth is, everyone has strengths to be recognized and areas where they can grow. Your role as a tech lead is to observe, acknowledge, and act on these moments.

每一天都藏着可以给反馈的机会；你只是需要留心。一旦你有意识地去寻找，就会开始注意到各种细节。事实是，每个人都有值得被认可的长处，也有可以成长的空间。作为技术负责人，你的职责就是观察这些时刻、认可它们，并据此行动。

If you're struggling to find feedback, start by reflecting on the behaviors that trigger strong reactions in you. Are there moments that frustrate you or make you uncomfortable? For instance, maybe in planning sessions, the product manager always asks, "Who wants to work on this ticket?" and the same few people always jump in, while others rarely volunteer and end up with little to do. Over time, this kind of imbalance can lead to tension or disengagement within the team, and it creates more work for you as those left out frequently ask for new tasks mid-sprint. Even just opening the conversation with the manager by pointing this out can lead to a more inclusive task assignment process. Together, you might explore new approaches that ensure everyone gets equal opportunities to contribute.

如果你苦于找不到可给的反馈，那就先从反思那些会激起你强烈反应的行为开始。有没有哪些时刻让你沮丧、或让你不舒服？例如，在计划会上，产品经理总是问："谁想接这个工单？"而总是那几个人主动跳进来，另一些人则很少请缨、结果没什么事可做。久而久之，这种失衡会在团队里造成紧张或 disengaged 的氛围，还会给你添更多活——因为那些被冷落的人会经常在迭代中途找你要新任务。哪怕只是向经理解开这个话题、把这个现象点出来，都可能带来一个更包容的任务分配流程。你们可以一起探索新的做法，确保每个人都有平等的贡献机会。

— PDF p.146 —

At the same time, take note of the positive actions that might otherwise go unnoticed. Maybe a team member consistently takes on tasks no one else volunteers for, or someone always steps up to help a colleague who's stuck. Even when it's part of their role, these efforts deserve recognition. Highlighting these actions shows your team that you value and appreciate their contributions, no matter how small they may seem.

与此同时，也要留意那些本可能被忽略的积极举动。也许某位团队成员总是主动接下没人愿意认领的任务，或者总有人在同事卡住时站出来帮忙。哪怕这些本就是他们职责的一部分，这些付出也值得被认可。点出这些行为，是在向团队表明：无论看起来多么微小，你都看重并感激他们的贡献。

To ensure you always have meaningful feedback to give, start keeping a record of your observations. Jot down what you notice: when and where something happened, what was said or done, how it made you feel, and the impact it had on you, the team, or the clients. This helps you stay prepared for feedback sessions by building a history of examples. Over time, this makes it easier to follow up on positive behaviors you want to reinforce or areas that need improvement.

为了确保自己总有有意义的反馈可给，开始把你的观察记录下来。草草记下你注意到的：事情发生在何时何地、说了什么或做了什么、它让你有什么感受、以及它对你、团队或客户产生了什么影响。这能帮你积累下一份"事例档案"，让你在反馈沟通时有所准备。久而久之，无论是想强化的积极行为，还是需要改进的方面，跟进起来都会更容易。

Once you start paying attention and documenting what you see, you'll quickly realize you're never out of feedback. The key is to look, listen, and be intentional. There's always something to acknowledge, whether it's to celebrate progress or address challenges.

一旦你开始留心、并把所见记录下来，就会很快意识到：你从来不会缺反馈可给。关键在于去看、去听、并带着意图。总有值得认可的事情——无论是庆祝进展，还是应对挑战。

"I CANNOT GET MY TEAM TO GIVE ME CONSTRUCTIVE FEEDBACK""我没法让团队给我建设性反馈"

Getting constructive feedback from your team can be challenging. Fear of your reaction, worries about damaging relationships, or concerns about how their honesty might affect their growth often hold people back. Building trust is essential, as discussed in Chapter 3. Beyond that foundation, here are a variety of strategies you can use to encourage your team to provide you with useful feedback:

从团队那里获得建设性反馈可能颇具挑战。人们之所以却步，往往是因为害怕你的反应、担心破坏关系，或顾虑自己的坦诚会如何影响到个人成长。正如第 3 章所讨论的，建立信任是根本。在这个基础之上，下面是一系列策略，可以用来鼓励团队给你提供有用的反馈：

Display vulnerability展露脆弱

When it comes to feedback, vulnerability can be your most powerful tool. Openly admit areas where you know you can improve. For example, say, "This is a topic where I know I have room to grow. Do you have any ideas on what I should start or stop doing to get better at this?" When you show that you're open to improvement, it makes it easier for your team to be honest, as you've already done the hard part: acknowledging the area of improvement.

在反馈这件事上，脆弱可能是你最有力的工具。坦然承认那些你知道自己可以改进的方面。例如说："在这个话题上，我知道自己还有成长空间。对于我该开始做什么、停止做什么，你有什么想法吗？"当你展现出对改进持开放态度时，团队就更容易对你坦诚——因为最难的那一步（承认自己有可改进之处），你已经替他们走完了。

— PDF p.147 —

Use structured input采用结构化的输入

Share a list of role expectations and ask team members to highlight three things you're doing well and three areas for improvement. This clear framework makes it easier for them to provide actionable feedback.

分享一份"岗位期望"清单，请团队成员标出三件你做得好的事、以及三个可改进的方面。这个清晰的框架，让他们更容易给出可落地的反馈。

Focus on specific situations聚焦具体情境

Reflecting on specific moments that didn't go as planned is a highly effective way to encourage constructive feedback. For example, you can ask, "What do you think about the way I handled that situation? What could I have done differently?" By acknowledging that the situation didn't go smoothly, you're signaling to your team that you're open to critique and actively seeking to improve.

回想那些没能按计划走的具体时刻，是鼓励建设性反馈的一种高效方式。例如你可以问："你觉得我处理那件事的方式怎么样？我本可以怎么做？"通过承认那件事办得不顺，你就在向团队传递一个信号：你乐于接受批评、并在主动寻求改进。

This approach reduces the pressure on them to identify flaws, as the example is already on the table. If their response is overly positive despite a clear misstep, it might indicate a lack of trust or hesitation to deliver tough feedback, which is a sign that there's more work to do in building psychological safety within your team.

这种做法减轻了他们"去挑毛病"的压力，因为例子已经摆到台面上了。如果你明明明显搞砸了一件事，他们的回应却过分正面，那可能意味着信任不足、或他们不敢给出刺耳的反馈——这是一个信号：你在团队内建立心理安全方面，还有更多工作要做。

Ask for anonymous feedback征求匿名反馈

Provide an alternative channel for feedback, like an anonymous form. This can encourage those who feel hesitant to speak up directly to share their insights. To make these forms truly effective, include open-ended, thoughtful questions that invite reflection and specificity. For example: "What's one thing I should start doing to better support the team?"

提供一个反馈的替代渠道，比如一份匿名表单。这能鼓励那些不好意思当面直说的人分享他们的见解。要让这些表单真正有效，就要加入开放式、需要思考的问题，引导对方反思并给出具体内容。例如："为了更好地支持团队，我应该开始做哪一件事？"

That said, anonymous feedback has its limitations. You can't easily follow up to clarify or dive deeper. In small teams, it's often possible to guess who submitted the feedback, which can erode trust. And if overused, it might reinforce a culture of avoidance rather than openness. Use it as a supportive tool to get people sharing but not as a substitute for a proper feedback conversation.

话虽如此，匿名反馈也有局限。你很难跟进去澄清或深挖。在小团队里，往往能猜到是谁提交的，这反而会侵蚀信任。而且如果用得太滥，它可能强化的是一种回避文化，而非开放文化。把它当作一个鼓励大家开口的辅助工具，而不是一次正式反馈谈话的替代品。

Go first率先开口

There's often that awkward pause at the start of a feedback session: "Do you want to go first?" "No, you go." Instead of waiting it out, take the lead. Just say, "I can go first, if it's the same to you." Starting with your own feedback, especially something thoughtful and focused on growth, can make the other person feel more comfortable and open to sharing feedback with you in return.

反馈沟通一开始，常常会出现一阵尴尬的停顿："你想先来吗？""不，你先来。"与其干等着，不如你来带头。就说一句："如果你不介意，我可以先来。"先给出你自己的反馈——尤其是那种经过深思、聚焦成长的反馈——能让对方更放松，也更愿意反过来和你分享。

— PDF p.148 —

Ask targeted questions提出有针对性的问题

Sometimes the key to unlocking useful feedback is to make it as easy as possible for your team to respond. Frame your request in specific, manageable terms, such as "What is one thing I should improve at?" or "What is one thing I can do to better support you?" Another effective question is "What is one thing I should start doing as a tech lead?" These focused and direct questions simplify the process for your team, guiding their thoughts and making it less intimidating to share feedback.

有时候，解锁有用反馈的关键，在于让团队尽可能轻松地作答。把你的请求框定成具体、力所能及的说法，比如"有哪一件事是我应该改进的？"或"我可以做哪一件事来更好地支持你？"另一个有效的问题是："作为技术负责人，有哪件事是我应该开始做的？"这些聚焦而直接的问题，简化了团队的作答过程，引导他们的思路，也让分享反馈不那么令人生畏。

Don't call it feedback别叫它“反馈”

Sometimes, the word feedback itself can feel intimidating, especially in formal settings. Instead, approach the topic casually by asking about specific events. After a challenging conversation, you might say, "How do you think that conversation went?" Similarly, following a presentation, you could ask, "What did you think about my presentation?" By focusing on the situation rather than labeling it as feedback, you create a more relaxed and open environment, encouraging honest and constructive input without the extra pressure.

有时候，"反馈"这个词本身就会让人发怵，尤其是在正式场合。不如换个轻松的方式，就具体的事件来聊。在一次艰难的谈话之后，你可以问："你觉得刚才那场谈得怎么样？"同样，在一次汇报之后，你可以问："你觉得我刚才的汇报怎么样？"通过聚焦具体情境、而不是给它贴上"反馈"的标签，你就营造了一个更放松、更开放的氛围，在没有额外压力的情况下，鼓励对方给出诚实而建设性的意见。

Getting useful feedback from your team won't happen overnight. It takes consistency, intention, and a willingness to show up vulnerably. These strategies can help you encourage your team to start giving you constructive feedback more openly and quickly, but there's no one-size-fits-all approach. Try them at different times, with different people. Each individual will respond differently, and it may take some experimentation to find what works best. What matters is that you keep trying. When your team sees that you genuinely care about growing, that you act on what you hear, and that their input has a real impact, they're far more likely to speak up.

从团队那里获得有用的反馈，不是一朝一夕的事。它需要持之以恒、带着意图、并愿意以脆弱的姿态出现。这些策略能帮你鼓励团队更开放、更迅速地开始给你建设性反馈，但没有放之四海而皆准的方法。在不同的时机、对不同的人多试几次。每个人的反应都不一样，可能需要一番摸索才能找到最有效的做法。重要的是你不断去试。当团队看到你是真的在乎成长、你会把听到的话付诸行动、他们的意见真的有影响时，他们就更有可能开口。

BUILDING A FEEDBACK CULTURE ON YOUR TEAM在团队中建立反馈文化

A team that embraces feedback bonds faster because it requires openness and vulnerability. Constructive feedback speeds up individual growth by providing clear improvement points. Positive feedback boosts morale, giving team members validation and reassurance that builds confidence and motivation.

一支拥抱反馈的团队，联结得更快，因为反馈本身就要求开放与脆弱。建设性反馈通过指明清晰的改进点，加速个人的成长。正面反馈提振士气，给团队成员以肯定和安心，从而建立信心与动力。
